title: Documenting a network experiment
goals: Record a network experiment with enough detail to replay its calculations
Trace reported metrics to data roles and saved parameters
Write a bounded conclusion and identify missing evaluation evidence

prerequisite.prompt: Why is “the model was fast and accurate” insufficient as an experiment record?
prerequisite.answer: It omits the task, data and splits, model and code versions, quality counts or loss definition, hardware, timing boundary and raw results. Another person cannot check what was measured or repeat the comparison.

vocabulary: A unique label linking one experiment’s settings, outputs and records
Saved model parameters at a specified stage of training
An inventory connecting named artifacts with versions, roles and integrity information
Repeating a recorded procedure to check whether its outputs agree

lesson.title: State a question and preserve the inputs

blocks.text: A useful experiment record explains what was asked, what was done, what happened and what remains unknown. Use run NN32-A: does fitting one positive ReLU weight reduce validation mean squared error compared with its initial value? This tiny constructed regression task teaches record keeping; it cannot establish performance on real-world data.

The network predicts max(0, a*x), with one weight a and no bias. Start at a = 1, use learning rate 0.1, two full-batch training updates and mean squared error, the mean of squared prediction errors. There is no normalisation, random initialisation or shuffling. Use Python float arithmetic and record the actual Python version when replaying.

Before running, set the selection rule: choose the checkpoint with the smaller validation MSE, breaking a tie toward the earlier update. The initial model is the baseline. Validation V1 chooses a checkpoint but never contributes to the training gradient. Final evaluation has not been run; its result must be recorded as not measured.

lesson.title: Keep a record of every update

blocks.text: For these two training cases, MSE = 2.5*(a - 2) squared and its gradient is 5*(a - 2). At a = 1 the gradient is -5, so the first update is 1 - 0.1*(-5) = 1.5. The next gradient is -2.5, giving a = 1.75. All preactivations in this run stay positive, so ReLU’s derivative is one; this is not a general backpropagation implementation.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The code assumes the supplied nonempty numeric datasets and positive preactivations. Each record stores update number, weight, training MSE and validation MSE after the update. Keep both records, the initial weight and the rule; saving only the best score erases how the choice was made.

lesson.title: Link a conclusion to its evidence

blocks.title: Read each checkpoint against the same validation case
blocks.caption: The baseline validation MSE is 9. The predeclared rule selects update 2 with validation MSE 0.5625 on one validation case. This is not a final-test score.

blocks.text: A defensible conclusion is: in run NN32-A, update 2 reduced MSE on the single constructed validation case from 9 to 0.5625 compared with the initial model. This checkpoint was selected using that same validation case; generalisation is untested. No timing, peak-memory or energy measurements are provided.

blocks.label: Using the selected weight, calculate the prediction for V1 and its squared error. Explain why the result must be labelled validation rather than independent final evaluation.

lesson.title: Package a record another person can inspect

blocks.text: Keep a manifest for the data with IDs and split membership, the exact code, settings, every checkpoint, raw prediction rows and metric calculations. Add run ID, author/date, environment versions, known data provenance and permitted use, failed attempts, decisions and limitations. A descriptive filename helps navigation, but does not prove that file contents stayed unchanged.

When saving artifacts, record their content hashes and keep the exact versions used. Hashes help detect content changes; they do not prove label correctness or experiment quality. Retain the input order, any training-fitted preprocessing, model architecture and numeric precision. Randomised experiments must also record seeds and the relevant random operations; a seed alone does not guarantee identical results across environments.

Ask a partner to replay from the record rather than from memory. If results differ, check inputs, split membership, preprocessing, configuration, code, parameters and environment. Document the discrepancy and the repair instead of overwriting the old record. A rerun on the same data checks the procedure; it does not add new independent evaluation cases.

lesson.title: Separate evidence from the next experiment

blocks.text: Report missing measurements as not measured, not as zero. If a final set has influenced a change, document that use and reserve new untouched evaluation before making an independent performance claim. A polished report cannot fix leakage or missing evidence. For larger experiments, preserve denominators, subgroup results and resource conditions from Weeks 29 to 31.

blocks.label: A report says “final accuracy 0.5625, low energy” but includes only the selected weight and no data or code. Repair its claim and name the minimum evidence needed to check this run.

blocks.text: Finish with a next action that follows from the limitations, such as planning a broader reserved evaluation without claiming it has already succeeded. Next week begins the capstone by defining a hypothesis and baseline before controlled experiments.

workbook.title: Write the replay settings
workbook.prompt: For NN32-A, record the prediction rule, initial weight, bias policy, learning rate, update count, loss, training/validation IDs, data order or shuffling policy, and checkpoint selection rule. Name one environment field still to record when you run it.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Predict max(0, a*x); start a = 1 with no bias; rate 0.1; two full-batch updates; MSE is mean squared prediction error. T1 and T2 train, V1 validates; no shuffling or normalisation. Select lower validation MSE, ties to earlier update. Record the actual Python version, alongside the code and Python float arithmetic.

workbook.title: Trace the selected result
workbook.prompt: Calculate both weight updates and give each training and validation MSE. Name the selected checkpoint and baseline validation MSE. How many independent validation examples support the comparison?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Weights are 1.5 then 1.75. Training MSE values are 0.625 and 0.15625; validation MSE values are 2.25 and 0.5625. Update 2 is selected; baseline validation MSE is 9. There is one validation example, not two examples created by evaluating two checkpoints.

workbook.title: Audit the artifact record
workbook.prompt: A folder contains only best-model.json and a screenshot of 0.5625. Identify four missing artifacts or records and explain what a content hash can and cannot verify.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Missing items include exact data with IDs and splits, code/configuration, earlier checkpoints, raw predictions and metric definitions, selection rule, and environment details. A hash can detect changes relative to recorded content; it cannot establish correct labels, sound splits or a valid conclusion.

workbook.title: Audit a new record independently
workbook.prompt: A separate run R17 records baseline a = 1 and checkpoints a = 1.5 and a = 1.75. It uses prediction max(0, a*x) and one validation case V9 with x = 4, y = 8. Compute baseline and checkpoint predictions and squared errors, choose by lowest validation MSE, and write a bounded conclusion. Final evaluation and runtime have not been measured.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Predictions are 4, 6 and 7; squared errors are 16, 4 and 1. Choose a = 1.75. In R17, that checkpoint lowers MSE on V9 from 16 to 1 relative to the baseline, but V9 also selects it. This is one-case validation evidence; final performance and runtime are not measured.

workbook.title: Investigate a replay mismatch
workbook.prompt: A partner gets different results after changing preprocessing and replacing the validation file. They keep the old run ID and overwrite the old score. Explain what should be preserved and how the revised work should be recorded.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Preserve the original data, preprocessing, settings, outputs and run ID. Compare exact artifact versions to identify the mismatch. Record changed preprocessing and data under a new run or explicit version, including reasons and results. A changed validation set is a different comparison; do not overwrite it as though it were the same run.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Treat the tiny ReLU model as a fully inspectable experiment, not a claim about real-world accuracy. The code trains one scalar on two rows and selects using one validation row. Require students to label metrics, denominators and data roles before judging the result; no final evaluation or resource measurement is supplied.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the missing details in a vague performance claim and introduce run NN32-A.
Read the data roles and configuration. Complete W1 with a replay settings record.
Trace the two gradient updates, optionally run the code, and complete W2.
Use the visual to connect parameters, predictions, metrics and the selection decision.
Complete the guided V1 calculation and distinguish replay from independent evidence.
Build an artifact manifest and complete W3, including the limits of hashes and seeds.
Collect W4 independently, requiring raw predictions, errors and a bounded validation claim.
Use W5 and the exit response to repair records. Give feedback, then administer the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: 1.75*3 = 5.25, error 5.25 - 6 = -0.75, squared error 0.5625. V1 selected the checkpoint and is validation, not untouched final evaluation. Exit: replace final accuracy with validation MSE 0.5625 on one constructed case selected using that case. Energy is not measured. Supply data and splits, exact code, settings, baseline and both checkpoints, raw predictions, metric definition, selection rule and environment information.
misconceptions: A smaller MSE is an accuracy percentage
MSE is an average squared error in squared target units; it is not classification accuracy or a percentage.
A replay adds new evaluation evidence
Reusing the same rows checks procedure consistency, not performance on new independent cases.
A seed or hash proves the experiment is sound
Seeds and hashes help track execution or integrity; they cannot repair bad labels, leakage or an unsupported claim.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires predictions 4, 6, 7 and squared errors 16, 4, 1; choose a = 1.75 and label the result one-case validation with final evaluation and runtime not measured. Fresh retry: R18 has the same baseline and checkpoints but validation x = 5, y = 10. Predictions are 5, 7.5, 8.75; squared errors are 25, 6.25, 1.5625. Choose a = 1.75. Require a validation-only conclusion and a record of which validation data version was used.
teacher.support: Provide a record frame with question, fixed settings, data roles, raw results, selection, limitations and next action. Allow a calculator and compare predictions before squared errors. Extension: rename a data file without changing its bytes, then edit a value; explain why only the content change alters its content hash. Use copies of fictional classroom data.
